title: Is there a natural limit?
summary: NH's long-form manifesto against the natural limit. He defines it as the point where progress becomes negligible, then argues it is mostly a product of height, genetics, poor programming, unwillingness to invest more time, cultural standards and YouTuber convenience. He says the concept promotes PED use and hopelessness, and that gains slow down but never stop.
claims: The natural limit is not a DNA-set ceiling on growth; that has never been proven by science and doesn't make logical sense
The defensible version of the natural limit is a threshold where the body resists adding muscle, strength and size plateau and progress becomes negligible
Shorter lifters reach what they call a limit faster because their potential for size was lower to begin with
A 6'7 lifter following the standards of a 5'6 man will never reach a tenth of his potential
Very tall natural lifters are the final frontier: so few have built size that nobody knows how big they can get
Genetically gifted lifters start higher, go higher and progress for longer; some made strength gains for three years on a minimalist linear program while others stalled after 6-7 months
Promises of a dream body in two months feed the natural-limit idea; real natural bodybuilding takes years
Nobody trains optimally at first; people claiming to be at their limit often have no program and don't know what volume is
Progression stops, not the training's ability to stimulate growth; change the stimulus and growth resumes
People who say nothing grows their calves just don't give them enough stimulus: heavy calf raises, negatives and loaded stretches will grow them
People claiming to be at their limit are usually far from it, for example guys benching 180 at 180 lb bodyweight after two years
The limit is chronological, not numerical: further progress needs more volume and frequency, meaning more time in the gym, which people don't want to invest
Refusing to spend the time a door takes to open doesn't mean it can't be opened
Numbers like 'a natural can't bench 400' or idolising the three-plate bench are subjective standards that create plateaus in your head
Testosterone matters less than people think; two people with the same test levels on the same routine won't grow equally
NH's theory: training makes natural lifters' bodies progressively more anabolic, so the hormonal profile and with it any 'limit' keeps evolving
Fixing body composition (too fat or too lean) improves hormones, so recomping can 'break' a supposed natural limit
Almost no naturals train rigorously for 10 uninterrupted years, so claims about a natural limit after 3-4 years have no valid evidence
Natural-limit talk pushes young men towards steroids, and the advised 'first cycle' point keeps creeping earlier, from 10 years down to 2
Juicers rationalise their health risk by claiming they couldn't progress naturally
Don't benchmark your progress against a YouTuber; you may have far more strength potential
Many fitness YouTubers stopped progressing to maintain and make money, and use the natural limit to excuse looking the same for five years
NH promises that if he spends a year in a plateau he'll call himself a failure rather than blame a natural limit
Doing PEDs 'to push past the limit then come off' fails: you regress after stopping, which shows the limit was never real
The natural limit is a cultural standard: in France people doubt NH is natural, in US gyms nobody does; if every man trained from 16 natural standards would skyrocket
Nobody claims a natural limit on reading speed, languages, tennis or running times, so why bodybuilding?
Comparing to others hurts both ways: a strong lifter with small shoulders may wrongly think he's at his limit despite strength to drive growth; a weaker one may give up
Inability to project years ahead feeds the natural-limit idea; over six weeks little changes, over three to five years you look different
Gains slow down but never stop, like a car going one mile per hour that still gets you far if you stay in it
Age-related decline arrives in your 50s-60s; in your 20s focus on the next 20 years of training
NH says he started training seriously only about three years earlier
